newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel plans to cede 40 pct of West Bank - paper.
newsitem.headline: Israel plans to cede 40 pct of West Bank - paper.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu has a secret plan to offer the Palestinians control of less than 40 percent of the West Bank in talks on a final peace accord, the newspaper Haaretz said on Thursday.

In Israeli radio interviews, Netanyahu acknowledged having some ideas about a final peace deal and said they were discussed in his inner cabinet for the first time on Wednesday when the military presented its security assessments.
He insisted -- despite a detailed map published alongside the story -- that: "There is no basis for this report because I haven't shown anyone or drafted any map."
But asked by Israel Radio if he had a map, Netanyahu replied: "A map in the head? Who doesn't have one?"

Palestinians have said that in final peace talks due to be completed by May 1999, they expect to get a far larger percentage of the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war and home to more than two million Palestinians.
Israel already has handed over much of the Gaza Strip, seven West Bank cities and part of an eighth to the Palestinians under peace deals launched in 1993.
"The secret map which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intends to present to the Palestinian Authority in final-status negotiations would give them less than 40 percent of the area," Haaretz said.

"The Palestinians will be told all the same that if the security situation will allow it over time, some security arrangements will be eased, and thus will the Palestinian entity get additional territories in the West Bank," said the report by military commentator Ze'ev Schiff.
His report said various details had yet to be worked out and the "Netanyahu map" was open to negotiation.

Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that as much as 60 percent of the West Bank would be turned over to the Palestinians under a proposal the security establishment presented to the cabinet ministers.
Asked which report to believe, Netanyahu told Israeli army radio: "I suggest that you not always believe what you read in the newspapers."
"I didn't specify any number." But he said: "I have my own ideas."
"We began a discussion yesterday in the inner cabinet -- an important discussion, perhaps among the most important ever to take place in Israeli governments," he told army radio.
"Certainly no such discussion has taken place since 1967 and it will continue during a series of meetings during which we will try to consolidate a proposal for a permanent arrangement," he said.
